name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 28

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: Admission of hospital worker or businessperson

blocks.note: first reading: what a hospital porter would say about himself
second reading: a trader who brings goods in from abroad

explanation.surface: Someone at a job interview confessing whether they work in a hospital or run a business.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whole spoken sentence, I'M PORTER, run together into one word; a porter wheels patients round a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: An importer is a trader whose business is buying goods from overseas to sell at home.

clue.text: Possibly people rowing across lake for fish

indicators.note: the rowers stretch across the next letter, so it sits within their word

blocks.note: people in boats, hinted at by 'possibly' since a boater could also be a hat
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A rowing crew crosses a lake to go fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: BOATERS goes round L, after its first letter. Bloaters are smoked herrings, a traditional British breakfast fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloater is a whole herring that has been salted and lightly smoked, so the plural names fish.

clue.text: Old geographer — around England's capital my plot is wrong

indicators.note: the scrambled words wrap around the capital letter, holding it inside them
a plot that is wrong is out of order, so its letters must be rearranged
'capital' keeps only the first letter of 'England'

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, rearranged
the capital, or first letter, of England

explanation.surface: An ancient map-maker complains that his scheme centred on England has gone awry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ptolemy was the second-century Alexandrian scholar whose Geography mapped the known world.

clue.text: Prayer is holding old man together

indicators.note: something holding another thing keeps it inside, so the short word goes within

blocks.note: taken as written
these letters wrap round the short word, but no standard reading of these clue words supplies them

explanation.surface: A prayer meeting keeps an elderly man in the family close.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and crossing letters fix the answer and IS clearly sits inside it, but the rest of the wordplay does not resolve cleanly; the printed clue may have lost a word.
explanation.definitionFit: An orison is an old literary word for a prayer, familiar from Hamlet.

clue.text: Judge society led by fools

indicators.note: being led by something means coming after it, which fixes the order of the two parts

blocks.note: asses are fools
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A complaint that the club's leadership is made up of idiots, so judge it accordingly.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to evaluate or form a judgement about something, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Tried idealism out with armies taken away

indicators.note: out here means put out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: every letter of these two words

explanation.surface: Idealism has been tried and abandoned now that the armed forces are gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A demilitarised zone or state has had its military forces removed, exactly what having armies taken away means.

clue.text: Sharp practice increased by 100% somewhere in London

blocks.note: adding a hundred per cent makes a thing twice as big
Ealing is a district of west London

explanation.surface: Some shady dealing has doubled the money somewhere in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The break in the answer falls one letter away from the break in the wordplay: DOUBLED and EALING join to form DOUBLE-DEALING.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-dealing is deceitful conduct, saying one thing and doing another, which is what sharp practice means.

clue.text: Conservative deeply stained

blocks.note: first meaning: set in one's ways, thoroughly traditional
second meaning: literally, wool dyed before spinning so the colour goes right through

explanation.walkthrough: The capital C suggests the political party, but it is just the general word for traditional.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone whose beliefs are fixed through and through, from yarn coloured before weaving.

clue.text: Gold and yellow round river with a sort of glow

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the colour word is read backwards

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
or is the heraldic name for gold or yellow
R is the abbreviation for river
taken as written

explanation.surface: A riverbank lit up in golden and yellow light.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' does double duty, ending the wordplay and opening the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aurora is the coloured glow of light seen in polar skies, such as the northern lights.

clue.text: Touring north-east, physician is one taking notice of folk

indicators.note: a tourer travels round a place, so the doctor goes round the compass letters

blocks.note: Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery
NE is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A doctor travelling round the north-east of England pays attention to the local people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folk' sounds like ordinary people, but it is folk music, which a listener attends to.
explanation.definitionFit: A listener is someone who pays attention to sound, here a person tuned in to folk music.

clue.text: The enemy losing a thousand in contest

indicators.note: something losing a part has that part taken away from it

blocks.note: time is called 'the enemy' in the old phrase about what wears everything down
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: An army loses a thousand soldiers in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time is the enemy' is a common saying; removing the Roman thousand leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is a match or contest in a knockout competition, as in a cup tie.

clue.text: 11_ — Silly person, the man in dress

blocks.note: a clot is British slang for a fool
the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A foolish fellow wearing a frock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but it only joins the wordplay to the definition, which is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To clothe someone is to put garments on them, the verb sense of dress.

clue.text: Maiden with strange actions in an all-male community

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, like the answer

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters fall into an unusual order

blocks.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
the letters of this word, rearranged

explanation.surface: A young woman behaving oddly in a community of men only.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden over in cricket is one with no runs scored; scorers write it M.
explanation.definitionFit: Monastic describes life in a monastery, a community made up entirely of monks.

clue.text: An attempt in the past

blocks.note: the article, written as a single letter
to have a go is to have an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone once had a try at something long since.
explanation.definitionFit: Ago places an event at an earlier time, so it means previously or in the past.

clue.text: Notice what someone wears and where they live

blocks.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a public notice
dress is clothing

explanation.surface: Pay attention to people's clothes and their homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: a printed advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Your address is the details of the house where you live, so it names a place of residence.

clue.text: Woman taken in by men always

indicators.note: something taken in by words is swallowed inside them, so look within the run of letters

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A woman is always being deceived by men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being fooled, but it means contained. ENA is a crossword staple woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ena is a woman's first name, as in Ena Sharples of the soap Coronation Street.

clue.text: A trick — Italian drug is poison!

blocks.note: taken as written
a con is a swindle or trick
It is the abbreviation for Italian
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A warning that some Italian's drug is really a toxic trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Aconite, or monkshood, is a plant whose roots yield a deadly toxin.

clue.text: Cleaner is a graduate — there's a certain attractiveness

blocks.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaner
taken as written
an MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady with a university degree turns out to have a special allure.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is an old British word for a woman paid to clean houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is a compelling personal charm that draws others, a particular kind of attractiveness.

clue.text: Piece of jewellery from exhibition centre Kay and Alec fashioned

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the name is worked into a new form

blocks.note: the NEC is the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham
kay is the spelt-out name of the letter K
the letters of this name, rearranged

explanation.surface: Two craftspeople, Kay and Alec, made a piece of jewellery shown at a trade fair.
explanation.walkthrough: Kay looks like a person's name but is the letter K spelt out; the NEC is Britain's big exhibition venue near Birmingham.
explanation.definitionFit: A necklace is an ornament worn round the neck, a kind of jewellery.

clue.text: Irritating framework

blocks.note: first meaning: harsh and annoying, like a rasping noise
second meaning: a grid of bars, as over a drain or fireplace

explanation.surface: An annoying piece of scaffolding.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for something that jars on the nerves and a noun for a lattice of metal bars.

clue.text: Mum's wise, having got right person to give treatment

blocks.note: Ma is mum, and the 's comes with her
sage means wise
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A wise mother has found the right therapist.
explanation.definitionFit: A massager rubs and kneads muscles, a person who gives physical treatment.

clue.text: Southern firm to employ someone from Merseyside

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
to employ something is to use it

explanation.surface: A company in the south of England takes on a Liverpudlian worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Merseyside is the area around Liverpool; Scouse is its dialect, and the word is also used for a Liverpudlian.
explanation.definitionFit: Scouse, short for Scouser, is an informal name for a native of Liverpool on Merseyside.

clue.text: Big gland has blood going round it

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: gore is spilt blood
taken as written

explanation.surface: An enlarged gland with blood circulating around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A goitre is a swelling of the thyroid, literally an enlarged gland in the neck.

clue.text: Bridges near Chester with bits falling off sides

indicators.note: bits falling off both sides means trimming letters from each end so only an inner run survives

blocks.note: the run of letters left once the ends are trimmed away

explanation.surface: Crumbling bridges near the city of Chester losing chunks from their sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Chester is a walled city in north-west England, chosen here for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An arch is the curved span of a bridge, and a bridge is often called arches when it has several.

clue.text: Port in which a song is heard

indicators.note: something heard reaches the ear, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A harbour town where music can be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayr is a harbour town on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayr is a Scottish seaport on the Firth of Clyde, so it is a port by name.

clue.text: 25__'~ Prank leading to awful riots? Strict person called for

indicators.note: awful means dreadful or wrecked, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: a rig is an old word for a trick or prank
the letters of this word, rearranged

explanation.surface: A practical joke sparks disorder, and a disciplinarian is summoned to restore order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Called for' completes the surface story and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigorist insists on strict observance of rules, a stickler for discipline.

clue.text: Homes made from soil go squishy

indicators.note: something squishy loses its shape, so the letters are squeezed into a new order

blocks.note: every letter of these two words

explanation.surface: Houses built of earth that turn to mush.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests mud huts, but the homes are made of snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Igloos are dome-shaped Inuit dwellings, so they are homes.

clue.text: Smashing gal, so romantic — such skill to produce wonderful food!

definitions.text: such skill to produce wonderful food
definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, describing such skill

indicators.note: smashing breaks a thing into pieces, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: every letter of these three words

explanation.surface: Praise for a lovely woman whose cooking is as romantic as she is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' reads as British praise for the girl, wonderful, but it signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastronomical relates to gastronomy, the art of preparing and enjoying fine cuisine.
